<div class="element-hidden">
  <div id="inline_content">
    <h1 id="transcript-top">Fundamentals of Physics I</h1>
    <h2>PHYS 200 - Lecture 6 - Law of Conservation of Energy in Higher Dimensions</h2>
    <p><h3>Chapter 1. Calculus Review: Small Changes for Motion in 2D [00:00:00]</h3><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> If you've got a function <em>f(x)</em>, you know the value at some point, and you want to go to a neighboring point, a distance <em> Δx</em> away. You ask, "How much does the function change?" And the answer is, the change in the function <em> Δf</em> is the derivative of the function at the starting point times the distance you move. This is not an equality, unless <em>f</em> happens to be a straight line; it's an approximation and there are corrections to this. That's what all the dots mean; corrections are proportional to <em> Δx2</em> and <em> Δx3</em> and so on. But if <em> Δx</em> is tiny this will do; that's it.</p><p>But today, we are going to move the whole Work Energy Theorem and the Law of Conservation of Energy to two dimensions. So, when you go to two dimensions, you've got to ask yourself, "What am I looking for?" Well, in the end, I'm hoping I will get some relation like <em>K1 + U1 = K2 + U2</em>, assuming there is no friction. <em>U2</em> is going to be my new potential energy. Then, if it's the potential energy and the particle is moving in two dimensions, it's got to be a function of two variables, <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>. So, I have to make sure that you guys know enough about functions of more than one variable. So, this is, again, a crash course on reminding you of the main points. There are not that many. By the time I get here I'll be done.</p><p>So, how do you visualize the function of two variables? The function of one variable, you know, you plot <em>x</em> this way and the function along <em>y</em>. If it's two variables, you plot <em>x</em> here and <em>y</em> here and the function itself is shown by drawing some surface on top of the <em>xy</em> plane, so that if you take a point and you go right up till you hit the surface, that's the value of the function, at that point <em>xy</em>. It's like a canopy on top of the <em>xy</em> plane and how high you've got to go is the function. For example, starting with the floor, I can ask how high you have to go till I hit the ceiling. That function varies; there are dents and dimples and so on, so the function varies with <em>xy</em>. Another example of a function of <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>--<em>x</em> and <em>y</em> could be coordinates in the United States and the function could be the temperature at that point. So, you plot it on top of that, each point you plot the temperature at that point.</p><p>So, once you've got the notion of a function of two variables, if you're going to do calculus the next thing is what about the derivatives of the function. How does it change? Well, in the old days, it was dependent on <em>x</em> and I changed the <em>x</em> and I found the change in the function divided by the change in <em>x</em> and took the limit and that became my derivative. And now, I'm sitting in the <em>xy</em> plane, so here is <em>x</em> and here is <em>y</em>; I'm here, the function is coming out of the blackboard. So, imagine something measured out but I'm sitting here. Now, I want to move and ask how the function changes. But now I have a lot of options; in fact, an infinite number of options. I can move along <em>x</em>, I can move along <em>y</em>, I can move at some intermediate angle, we have to ask what do you want me to do when it comes time to take derivatives. So, it turns out, and you will see it proven amply as we go along, that you just have to think about derivatives on two principle directions which I will choose to be <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>.</p><p>So, we're going to define one derivative, which is defined as follows. You start at the point <em>xy</em>, you go to the point <em>x</em> + <em> Δx</em>, the same <em>y</em> and subtract the function at the starting point, divide by <em> Δx</em> and take all the limits, <em> Δx</em> goes to 0. That means you go from here to here, you move a distance <em> Δx</em>, you'd find the change in the function, you take the derivative. As you move horizontally, you notice you don't do anything to <em>y</em>; <em>y</em> will be left fixed at whatever <em>y</em> you had; <em>x</em> will be changed by <em> Δx</em>; you find the change; you take the derivative and take the limit that is denoted by the symbol <em>df/dx.</em></p><p>[Reader note: Partial derivatives will be written as ordinary derivatives to avoid using fonts that may not be universally available. It should be clear from the context that a partial derivative is intended here, since <em>f</em> depends on <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>.]</p><p>So, this curly <em>d</em> instead of the straight <em>d</em> tells you it's called a "partial derivative." Some people may want to make it very explicit by saying this is the derivative with subscript <em>y</em>. That means <em>y</em> is being held constant when <em>x</em> is varied, but we don't have to write that because we know we've got two coordinates. If I'm changing one, the other guy is <em>y</em> so we won't write that; that's the partial derivative. So, you can also move from here to here, up and down, and see how the function changes. I won't write the details, you can define obviously a <em>df/dy</em>. So, one tells you how the function changes, with <em>x</em> I should move along <em>x</em>, and the other tells you how it changes at <em>y</em> as you move along <em>y</em>.</p><p>Let's get some practice. So, I'm going to write some function, <em>f = x3y2</em>, that's a function of <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>. You can write any--let's make it a little more interesting, plus <em>y</em>, or <em>y2</em>; that's some function of <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>. So, when I say <em>df/dx</em>, the rule is find out how it varies with <em>x</em> keeping <em>y</em> constant. That means, really treat it like a constant, because number five--What will you do if <em>y</em> was equal to 5? This'll be 25 and it's not part of taking derivatives because it's not changing, and here it'll be just standing in front doing nothing; it will just take the <em>x</em> derivative, treating <em>y</em> as a constant. You're supposed to do that here; this is a derivative 3<em>x2y</em>; so that's the <em>x</em> derivative. Now, you can take the <em>y</em> part, <em>y2</em>, yes, thank you. Then, I can take <em>df/dy</em>, so then I look for <em>y</em> changes, this is 2<em>y</em> here, so it's 2<em>x3y</em> + 2<em>y</em>; so that's the <em>x</em> derivative and the partial <em>y</em> derivative.</p><p>Okay, so then you can now take higher derivatives. We know that from calculus and one variable, you can take the derivative of the derivative. So, one thing you can think about is <em>d2f/dx2</em>, that really means take the <em>d</em> by <em>dx</em> of the <em>d</em> by <em>dx</em>. That's what it means. First, take a derivative and take the derivative of the derivative. So, let's see what I get here. I already took <em>df/dx</em>. I want to take its derivative, right, the derivative of <em>x2</em> is 2<em>x</em>, so I get 6<em>xy2</em>. Then, I can take the <em>y</em> derivative of the <em>y</em> derivative, <em>d2f/dy2</em>, that's <em>d</em> by <em>dy</em> of <em>df/dy</em>, if you take the <em>y</em> derivative there. You guys should keep an eye out for me when I do this. I get this. But now, we have an interesting possibility you didn't have in one dimension, which is to take the <em>x</em> derivative of the <em>y</em> derivative, so I want to take <em>d</em> by <em>dx</em> of <em>df/dy</em>. That is written as <em>d2f/dxdy</em>. Let's see what I get. So, I want the <em>x</em> derivative of the <em>y</em> derivative. So, I go to this guy and take his <em>x</em> derivative, I get 3<em>x2</em> from there, so I get 6<em>x2y</em> and that's it. So, make sure that I got the proper <em>x</em> derivative of this, I think that's fine. Then, I can also take <em>d2f/dydx</em>. That means, take the <em>y</em> derivative of the <em>x</em> derivative, but here's the <em>x</em> derivative, take the <em>y</em> derivative of that, put a 2<em>y</em> there, and I get 6<em>x2y</em>.</p><p>So, you're supposed to notice something. If you already know this, you're not surprised. If you've never seen this before, you will notice that the cross derivative, <em>y</em> followed by <em>x</em> and <em>x</em> followed by <em>y</em>, will come up being equal. That's a general property of any reasonable function. By reasonable, I mean you cannot call the mathematicians to help because they will always find something where this won't work, okay? But if you write down any function that you are capable of writing down with powers of <em>x</em> and powers of <em>y</em> and sines and cosines, it'll always be true that you could take the cross derivatives in either order and get the same answer. I'd like to give a little bit of a feeling for why that is true; it's true but it's helpful to know why it's true. So, let's ask the following question.</p><p>Let's take a function and let's ask how much the function changes when I go from some point <em>x</em>,<em>y</em> to another point <em>x</em> + <em> Δx</em>, <em>y</em> + <em> Δy</em>. I want to find the change in the function. So, I'm asking you what is <em>f(x + Δx, y + Δy) - f(x,y)</em> for small values of <em> Δx</em> and <em> Δy</em>. For neighboring points, what's the change? So, we're going to do it in two stages. We introduce an intermediate point here, whose coordinate is <em>x + Δ x</em> and <em>y</em>, and I'm going to add and subtract the value of the function here. Adding and subtracting is free; it doesn't cost anything, so let's do that. Then, what do I get? I get <em>f(x + Δx, y + Δy ) - f(x + Δx, y) + f(x + Δx, y) - f(x,y)</em>. I'm just saying, the change of that guy minus this guy is the same as that minus this, plus this minus that; that's a trivial substitution. But I write it this way because I look at the first entity here, it looks like I'm just changing <em>y</em>. I'm not changing <em>x</em>, you agree? So what will this be? This is going to be the rate of change of the function with respect to <em>x</em> times <em> Δx</em>, and this--I'm sorry, I got it wrong, with respect to <em>y</em> times <em> Δy</em>. This one is <em>df/dx</em> times <em> Δx</em>. Therefore, the change in the function, if I add it all up, I get <em>df/dx Δx + df/dy Δy</em>. But if you are pedantic, you will notice there is something I have to be a little careful about. What do you think I'm referring to, in my notation, yes?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> [inaudible]</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> Meaning?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> [inaudible]</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> Oh, but this is nothing to do with dimension, you see. It's one number minus another number. I put another number in between and in this function; it's a function only of here. Let me see, <em>x</em> is not changing at all and <em>y</em> is changing, so it is <em>df/dy Δy</em>. I meant something else. That is, in fact, a good approximation but there is one thing you should be careful about which has to do with where the derivatives are really taken. For the term here, <em>f(x + Δx, y) - f(xy)</em>, I took the derivative, at my starting point. If you want, I will say at the starting point <em>xy</em>. The second one, when I came here and I want to move up, I'm taking the derivative with respect to <em>y</em> at the new point. The new point is <em>(x + Δx, y)</em>, so derivatives are not quite taken at the same point. So, you've got to fix that. And how do you fix that part? You argue that the derivative with respect to <em>y</em> is just another function of <em>y</em>; <em>f</em> is a function of <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>, its derivatives are functions of <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>. Everything is a function of <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>, and we are saying this derivative has been computed at <em>x + Δx</em>, instead of <em>x</em>, so it is going to be <em>df/dy</em> at <em>xy</em> <em>+ d2f/dxdy</em> times <em> Δx</em>.</p><p>In other words, I am saying the derivative at this location is the derivative at that location, plus the rate of change of the derivative times the change in <em>x</em>. In other words, the derivative itself is changing. So, if you put that together you find it is <em>df/dx Δx + df/dy Δy</em>, where if I don't put any bars or anything it means at the starting point <em>xy + (d2f/dxdy) Δx Δy</em>. Now, you've got to realize that when you're doing these calculus problems, Δx is a tiny number, Δy is a tiny number, Δx Δy is tiny times tiny. So normally, we don't care about it, or if you want to be more accurate, of course, you should keep that term. In the first approximation, where you work to the first power of everything, this will be your <em> Δf</em>. But if you're a little more ambitious but you keep track of the fact the derivative itself is changing, you will keep that term.</p><p>But another person comes along and says, "You know what, I want to go like this. I want to introduce as my new point, intermediate point, the one here. It had a different value of <em>y</em> in the same <em>x</em> and then I went horizontally when I keep track of the changes." What do you think that person will calculate for the change in the function? That person will get exactly this part, but the extra term that person will get will look like <em>d2f/dydx</em> times <em> Δy Δx</em>. If you just do the whole thing in your head, you can see that I'm just exchanging the <em>x</em> and <em>y</em> roles. So, everything that happened with <em>x</em> and <em>y</em> here will come backwards with <em>y</em> and <em>x</em>. But then, the change between these two points is the change between these two points and it doesn't matter whether I introduce an intermediate point here or an intermediate point there; therefore, these changes have to be equal. This part is of course equal; therefore, you want that part to be equal, <em> Δx Δy</em> is clearly <em> Δy Δx</em>, so the consequence of that is <em>d2f/dxdy</em> = <em>d2f/dydx</em> and that's the reason it turns out when you take cross derivatives you get the same answer. It comes from the fact -- if you say, where is that result coming from -- it comes from the fact, if you start at some point and you go to another point and you ask for the change in the function, the change is accumulating as you move. You can move horizontally and then vertically, or you can move vertically and then horizontally. The change in the function is a change in the function. You've got to get the same answer both ways. That's the reason; that's the requirement that leads to this requirement.</p><p>Now, I will not be keeping track of functions to this accuracy in everything we do today. We'll be keeping the leading powers in <em> Δx</em> and <em> Δy</em>. So, you should bear in mind that if you make a movement in the <em>xy</em> plane, which is <em> Δx</em> horizontally and <em> Δy</em> vertically, then the change in the function is this [<em>df/dx Δx + df/dy Δy</em>]. Draw a box around that, because that's going to be--This is just the naïve generalization to two dimensions of what you know in one dimension. We were saying look, the function is changing because the independent variables <em>x</em> and <em>y</em> are changing, and the change in the function is one part, which I blame on the changing <em>x</em>, and a second part, which I blame on the changing <em>y</em> and I add them. So, you're worried about the fact that we're moving in the plane and there are vectors. That's all correct, but <em>f</em> is not a vector, <em>f</em> is just a number and this change has got two parts, okay. So, this is basically all the math we will need to do, what I want to do today.</p><h3>Chapter 2. Work Done in 2D; Dot Products and Cross Products [00:18:05]</h3><p>So, let's now go back to our original goal, which was to derive something like the Law of Conservation of Energy in two dimensions instead of one. You remember what I did last time so I will remind you one more time what the trick was. We found out that the change in the kinetic energy of some object is equal to the work done by a force, which was some <em>F</em> times <em> Δx</em> and then if you add all the changes over a not infinitesimal displacement, but a macroscopic displacement, that was given by integral of <em>F</em> times <em>dx</em> and the integral of <em>F</em> times <em>dx</em> from <em>x1</em> to <em>x2</em>. If <em>F</em> is a function only of <em>x</em>, from the rules of calculus, the integral can be written as a difference of a function at this limit minus that limit, and that was <em>U(x1) - U(x2)</em>, where <em>U</em> is that function whose derivative with a minus sign is <em>F</em>. That's what we did. Then, it's very simple now to take the <em>U1</em> to the left-hand side. Let me see, <em>K1</em> to the right-hand side and <em>U(x2)</em> to the left-hand side, to get <em>K2 + U2 = K1 + U1</em> and that's the conservation of energy.</p><p>You want to try the same thing in two dimensions; that's your goal. So, the first question is, "What should I use for the work done?" What expression should I use for the work done in two dimensions, because the force now is a vector; force is not one number, it's got an <em>x</em> part and a <em>y</em> part. My displacement has also got an <em>x</em> part and a <em>y</em> part and I can worry about what I should use. So, I'm going to deduce the quantity I want to use for <em> ΔW</em>, namely, the tiny work done which is an extension of this. I'm going to demand that since I'm looking for a Work Energy Theorem, I'm going to demand that, remember in one dimension <em> ΔK = F Δx</em>. If we divide it by the time over which it happens, I find <em>dK/dt</em> is equal to force [F] times velocity [v].</p><p>I'm going to demand that that's the power, force times velocity, is what I call the power. And I'm going to look for <em>dK/dt</em> in two dimensions, of a body that's moving. What's the rate at which kinetic energy is changing when a body is moving? For that, I need a formula for kinetic energy. A formula for kinetic energy is going to be again ½ <em>mv2</em>. I want that to be the same entity, so I will choose it to be that, but <em>v2</em> has got now <em>vx2</em> <em>+ vy2</em>, because you know whenever you take a vector <em>V</em>, then its length is the square root of the <em>x</em> part squared plus the <em>y</em> part squared. Any questions? Okay, so let's take the rate of change of this, <em>dK/dt</em>. Again, you have to know your calculus. What's the time derivative of <em>vx2</em>? The rule from calculus says, first take the derivative of <em>vx2</em> with respect to <em>vx</em>, which is 2<em>vx</em>, then take the derivative of <em>vx</em> with respect to time. So, you do the same thing for the second term, 2 <em>vy dvy/dt</em>, and that gives me--the 2s cancel, gives me <em>mdvx /dtvx + m dvy /dtvy</em>. This is the rate at which the kinetic energy of a body is changing. So, what's my next step, yes?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> So what happened to the half?</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> The half got canceled by the two here. Yes?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> [inaudible]</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> That's correct. So, what we want to do is to recognize this as <em>ma</em> in the <em>x</em> direction, because <em>m</em> times <em>dvx/dt</em> is <em>ax</em>, and this is <em>m</em> times <em>ay</em>. Therefore, they are the forces in the <em>x</em> and <em>y</em> directions, so I write <em>Fxvx + Fyvy</em>. So the power, when you go to two dimensions, is not very different from one dimension. In one dimension, you had only one force and you had only one velocity. In two dimensions, you got an <em>x</em> and <em>y</em> component for each one, and it becomes this. So, this is what I will define to be the power. When a body is moving and a force is acting on it, the force has two components, the velocity has two components; this combination shall be called "Power." But now, let's multiply both sides by <em> Δt</em> and write the change in kinetic energy is equal to <em>Fx</em> and you guys think about what happens when I multiply <em>vx</em> by <em> Δt</em>; <em>vx</em> = <em>dx/dt</em>. Multiplying by <em> Δt</em> just gives me the distance traveled in the <em>x</em> direction <em>+ Fy</em> times <em>dy</em>. So, this is the tiny amount of work done by a force and it generalizes what we had here, work done is force times <em> Δx</em>. In two dimensions, it's <em>Fxdx + Fydy</em>. It's not hard to guess that but the beauty is--this combination--Now you can say, you know what, I didn't have to do all this, I could have always guessed that in two dimensions, when you had an <em>x</em> and a <em>y</em> you obviously have to add them. There's nothing very obvious about it because this combination is now guaranteed to have the property that if I call this the work done. Then, it has the advantage that the work done is in fact the change in kinetic energy.</p><p>I want to define work so that its effect on kinetic energy is the same as in 1D, namely, work done should be equal to change in kinetic energy. And I engineered that by taking the change in kinetic energy, seeing whatever it came out to, and calling that the work done, I cannot go wrong. But now, if you notice something repeating itself all the time, which is that I had a vector <em>F</em>, which you can write as <em>I</em> times <em>Fx + J</em> times <em>Fy</em>, I had a vector velocity, which is <em>I</em> times <em>vx + J</em> times <em>vy</em>. Then, I had a tiny distance moved by the particle, which is <em>I</em> times <em>dx + J</em> times <em>dy</em>. So, the particle moves from one point to another point. The vector describing its location changes by this tiny vector. It's just the step in the <em>x</em> direction times <em>I</em>, plus step in the <em>y</em> direction times <em>J</em>. So, what you're finding is the following combination. The <em>x</em> component of <em>F</em> times the <em>x</em> component of <em>v</em>, plus the <em>y</em> component of <em>F</em>, times the <em>y</em> component of <em>v</em>. Or <em>F</em> component of <em>x</em> times the distance moved in <em>x</em> plus <em>y</em> component of <em>F</em> times the displacement in <em>y</em>.</p><p>So, we are running into the following combination. We are saying, there seem to be in all these problems two vectors, <em>I</em> times <em>Ax + J</em> times <em>Ay</em>. <em>A</em>, for example, could be the force that I'm talking about. There's another vector <em>B</em>, which is <em>I</em> times <em>Bx + J</em> times <em>By</em>. Right? For example, this guy could be standing in for <em>F</em>, this could be standing in for <em>v</em>. The combination that seems to appear very naturally is the combination <em>AxBx + AyBy</em>. It appears too many times so I take it seriously, give that a name. That name will be called a dot product of <em>A</em> with <em>B</em> and is written like this. Whenever something appears all the time you give it a name; this is <em>A.B.</em> So, for any two vectors <em>A</em> and <em>B</em>, that will be the definition of <em>A.B</em>. Then, the work done by a force <em>F</em>, that displaces a particle by a tiny vector <em>dr</em>, is <em>F.dr</em>. The particle's moving in the <em>xy</em> plane. From one instant to the next, it can move from here to there. That little guy is <em>dr</em>; it's got a little bit horizontal and it's got a little bit vertical, that's how you build <em>dr</em>. The force itself is some force which at that point need not point at the direction in which you're moving. It's some direction. At each point, the force could have whatever value it likes.</p><p>So, the dot product, you know, sometimes you learn the dot product as <em>AxBx + AyBy</em>, you can ask, "Who thought about it?" Why is it a natural quantity? And here is one way you can understand why somebody would think of this particular combination.</p><p>So, once you've got the dot product, you've got to get a feeling for what it is. The first thing we realize is that if you take a dot product of <em>A</em> with itself, then it's <em>AxAx + AyAy</em>, which is <em>Ax2 + Ay2</em>, which is the length of the vector <em>A</em>, which you can either denote this way or just write it without an arrow. So <em>A.A</em> is a positive number that measures the length squared of the vector <em>A</em>, likewise <em>B.B</em>. Now, we have to ask ourselves, "What is <em>A.B</em>?" So, somebody know what <em>A.B</em> is? Yep?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> [inaudible]</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> Okay, so how do we know that? How do we know it's length of <em>A</em> times length of <em>B</em> times cosine of the angle? You should follow from--Is it an independent definition or is it a consequence of this? Yep?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> Well, you can derive using the Law of Cosines.</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> Yes. He said we can derive it using the Law of Cosines and that's what I will do now. In other words, that definition which you may have learnt about first is not independent of this definition; it's a consequence of this definition. So, let's see why that's true. Let's draw two vectors here. Here is <em>A</em> and here is <em>B</em>, it's got a length <em>A</em>, it's got a length <em>B</em>, this makes an angle, <em>θA</em> with the <em>x</em> axis, and that makes an angle <em>θB</em> for the <em>x</em> axis. Now, do you guys agree that the <em>x</em> component of <em>A</em> with the horizontal part of <em>A</em> is the <em>A</em> <em>cos θA</em>? You must've seen a lot of examples of that when you did all the force calculation. And <em>Ay</em> is equal to the length of <em>A</em> times <em>sin θA</em> and likewise for <em>B</em>; I don't feel like writing it. If you do that, then <em>A.B</em> will be length of <em>A</em>, length of <em>B</em> times <em>(cos θA cos θB + sin θA sin θB)</em>.</p><p>You've got to go back to your good old trig and it'll tell you this <em>cos cos</em> plus <em>sin sin is cos (θA - θB)</em>.So, you find it is length of <em>A</em>, length of <em>B</em>, <em>cos (θA - θB)</em>. Often, people simply say that is <em>AB cos θ</em>, where it's understood that <em>θ</em> is the angle between the two vectors. So, the dot product that you learnt--I don't know which way it was introduced to you first, but these are two equivalent definitions of the dot product. In one of them, if you're thinking more in terms of the components of <em>A</em>, a pair of numbers for <em>A</em> and a pair of numbers for <em>B</em>, this definition of the dot product is very nice. If you're thinking of them as two little arrows pointing in different directions, then the other definition, in which the lengths and the angle between them appear, that's more natural. But numerically they're equal. An important property of the dot product, which you can check either way, is the dot product of <em>A</em> with <em>B + C</em>, is dot product of <em>A</em> with <em>B</em> plus dot product of <em>A</em> with <em>C</em>. That just means you can open all the brackets with dot products as you can with ordinary products. Now, that's a very important property of the dot product. So, maybe I can ask somebody, do you know one property, significant property of the dot product?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> When two vectors are perpendicular the dot product equals 0.</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> Oh that's interesting, I didn't think about it. Yes. One thing is if two vectors are perpendicular the dot product is 0 because the cosine of 90 is 0. But what I had in mind--Of course it's hard for me, it's not fair I ask you some question without saying what I'm looking for. What can you say if you use a different set of axis? Yep?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> In this case it doesn't matter.</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> If you go to the rotated axis, the components of vector <em>A</em> will change. We have done that in the homework; we've done that in the class. The components of <em>B</em> will also change. Everything will get a′. But the combination, <em>AxBx + AyBy</em>, when you evaluate it before or after, will give the same answer because it's not so obvious when you write it this way. But it's very obvious when you write it this way because it's clear to us if you stand on your head or you rotate the whole axis. What you're looking for is the length of <em>A</em>, which certainly doesn't change on your orientation, or the length of <em>B</em>, or the angle between them. The angle <em>θA</em> will change but the angle with the new <em>x</em> axis won't be the same. The angle with the new <em>y</em> axis won't be the same. Likewise for <em>B</em>, but the angle between the vectors, it's an invariant property, something intrinsic to the two vectors, doesn't change, so the dot product is an invariant. This is a very important notion. When you learn relativity, you will find you have one observer saying something, another observer saying something. They will disagree on a lot of things, but there are few things they will all agree on. Those few things will be analog of <em>A.B</em>. So, it's very good to have this part of it very clear in your head. This part of elementary vector analysis should be clear in your head.</p><p>Okay, so any questions about this? So, if you want, geometrically, the work done by a force when it moves a body a distance <em>dr</em>, a vector <em>dr</em>, is the length of the force, the distance traveled, times the cosine of the angle between the force and the displacement vector.</p><p>Okay, I'm almost ready for business because, what is my goal? On the left-hand side, the <em> ΔK</em>s, this whole thing was defined so that it's equal to <em> ΔK</em>, right? <em> ΔK</em> was equal to this, that's equal to all that. So, if you add all the <em> ΔK</em>s, it's very clear what you will get. You will get the kinetic energy at the end minus kinetic energy at the beginning. That just means, if you want to go from <em>A</em> to <em>B</em> along some path, you chop up the path into tiny pieces. Each tiny segment, if it's small enough to be approximated by a tiny vector <em>dr</em>, then take the dot product of that little <em>dr</em>, with the force at that point, which means length of <em>F</em>, times the length of the segment, times cosine of the angle; add them all up. Then somebody will say, "Well, your segments are not short enough for me." We'll chop it up some more, then chop it up some more, chop it up till your worst critic has been silenced. That's the limit in which you can write the answer as this integral. Just like in calculus when you integrate a function you take tiny intervals <em> Δx</em>, multiply <em>F</em> by <em> Δx</em>, but then you make the intervals more and more numerous but less and less wide and the limit of that is the area under the graph and that's called "integral," you do the same thing now in two dimensions.</p><h3>Chapter 3. <article data-history-node-id="1557" class="node session-full node--type-session node--promoted node--view-mode-full">
	<div class="node__content session-full__content">
		<h2 class="session-full__title">
			Lecture 8
			-
			Dynamics of a Multiple-Body System and Law of Conservation of Momentum
		</h2>
		<div class="session-full__body">
			<h3 class="session-full__body-label">
				Overview
			</h3>
			<p>The dynamics of a many-body system is examined. Through a variety of examples, the professor demonstrates how to locate the center of mass and how to evaluate it for a number of objects. Finally, the Law of Conservation of Momentum is introduced and discussed. The lecture ends with problems of collision in one dimension focusing on the totally elastic and totally inelastic cases.</p>
		</div>

    <h1 id="transcript-top">Fundamentals of Physics I</h1>
    <h2>PHYS 200 - Lecture 8 - Dynamics of a Multiple-Body System and Law of Conservation of Momentum</h2>
    <p><h3>Chapter 1. Multibody Dynamics — The Two-Body System [00:00:00]</h3><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> So, today we are going to do something different from what's happened so far, in that we are going to study the dynamics of more than one body. Well, you might say "Look, we already did this last week, when I studied the Solar System," where there are planets moving around the Sun so that makes at least two bodies, the Sun and the planet. But actually, the Sun was not doing anything interesting in our analysis. The Sun just stood there as a source of the gravitational force. It's the planet that did all the orbiting and that was the problem in two dimensions, but of only one body. So now, we are going to enlarge our domain to more than one body obeying Newton's laws.</p><p>So, let me start with the simplest possible case: two bodies. And I will again start with the simplest case of their moving in one dimension; then, we'll put in more. So, here is the one-dimensional world in which these bodies are going to move, and this is my origin, <em>x</em> = 0, and I'm going to imagine one point mass <em>m1</em>, located at <em>x1</em>, another point mass <em>m2</em>, located at <em>x2</em>. Now, we know everything there is to know about these masses from the laws of Newton which I'm going to write down. The first mass obeys this equation, <em>m1d2x1/ dt2</em>. That's <em>ma</em>, right? But I'm going to write this in a notation that's more succinct. I'm tired of writing the second derivative in this fashion. I'm going to write it as follows, <em>m1x1</em>, with two dots on it; the two dots telling you it's two derivatives, because one dot is one derivative, three dots is three derivatives. Of course, at some point this notation becomes unwieldy, but you never deal with more than two derivatives, so this works. This is <em>ma</em>, so don't forget the dots, okay? This is not some foreign alphabet. Every dot is a derivative. You should remember that when I do subsequent manipulation. That's <em>ma</em>, and that's equal to force on body 1, <em>F1</em>.</p><p>Now, look at the body one and ask, "What are the forces acting on it?" Well, it could be the whole universe. But we're going to divide that into two parts. The first part is going to be the force on body 1 due to body 2, which I'm going to denote by <em>F12</em>; that's our notation. You and I agree that it's the force on 1 due to 2. Then, there's the force on 1 due to the external world; <em>e</em> stands for external. That means everything outside these two. So, the universe has many bodies; I have just picked these two guys. They're 1 and 2, and the force on 1 is--some of it's due to 2, and some of it's due to everything else.</p><p>Similarly, I have another equation, <em>m2x2</em> double dot is the force on 2 due to 1 plus the force on 2 due to the outside world. What do you mean by "outside world"? Maybe these two guys are next to some planet, and the planet's way over to the right, it's pulling all of them towards the planet with some gravitational force. So, everything else is called "external." And I have 1 and 2, for example, are connected by a spring. The spring is not that important. It's a way of transmitting force from one body to the other. If you compress the spring and let it go, these two masses will vibrate back and forth under the influence of the other person's force. That's an example of <em>F12</em> and <em>F21</em>. For example, if the spring is compressed at this instant, it's trying to push them out; that means, really, 1 is trying to push 2 out, whereas that way 2 is trying to push 1 to the left, this way. That's an example of <em>F12</em> and <em>F21</em>.</p><p>The external force could be due to something extraneous to these two bodies. So, one example is at the surface of the Earth. I take these two masses connected by a spring. Here is mass 1 and here's mass 2. I squash the spring. If there is no gravity, they will just go vibrating up and down but let them fall into the field of gravity, so they're also experiencing the <em>mg</em> due to gravity. So, they will both fall down and also oscillate a little with each other. They're all described by this equation. This will be the spring force transmitted from 1 to 2. This will be the force of gravity, or it could be an electric force or any other force due to anything else; we are not interested.</p><p>Now, here is the interesting manipulation we're going to perform. We are going to add the two things on the left-hand side and equate them to whatever I get on the right-hand side. Then, <em>m1x1</em> double dot plus <em>m2x2</em> double dot, and that's going to be--I'm going to write it in a particular way, <em>F1e + F2e + F12 + F21</em>. I think you have some idea of where I'm headed now. So, what's the next thing we could say? Yes?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> <em>F12 + F21</em> = 0.</p><h3>Chapter 2. The Center of Mass [00:05:41]</h3><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> Yes, because that's the Third Law of Newton. Whatever the underlying force, gravity, spring, anything, force on 1 due to 2, and force on 2 due to 1 will cancel, and everything I get today, the whole lecture is mainly about this one simple result, this cancellation. Then, this whole thing, I'm going to write as <em>Fe</em>, meaning the total external force on this two-body system. So, I have this peculiar equation. I'm going to rewrite it in a way that brings it to the form in which it's most useful. I'm going to introduce a new guy, capital <em>X</em>. As you know, that's called a center of mass coordinate, and it's defined as <em>m1x1 + m2x2</em> divided by capital <em>M</em>. Capital <em>M</em> is just the total mass, <em>m1 + m2</em>. If I do that, this is a definition. Then, we can write this equation as follows. I will write it and then we can take our time seeing that it is correct. So, this is really the big equation. Why don't you guys try to fill in the blanks in your head? This is really correct. On the left-hand side, I have <em>M</em> times <em>X</em> double dot, so I have really <em>m1 + m2</em> times <em>X</em> double dot. If you take the double dot of this guy, it's <em>m1x1</em> double dot plus <em>m2x2</em> double dot, divided by <em>m1 + m2</em>. So, the left-hand side is indeed this; that's all I want you to check. So, take this expression, divide by the total mass and multiply by the total mass. Well, the multiplying by the total mass is here, and when you divide by the total mass you get the second derivative of the center of mass coordinate.</p><p>So what have I done? I have introduced a fictitious entity, the center of mass. The center of mass is a location <em>X</em>, some kind of a weighted average of <em>x1</em> and <em>x2</em>. By weighted, I mean if <em>m1</em> and <em>m2</em> are equal, then capital <em>M</em> will be two times that mass and you'll just get <em>x1 + x2</em> over 2. The center of mass will sit right in between. But if <em>m1</em> is heavier, it'll be tilted towards <em>m1</em>; if <em>m2</em> is heavier, it'll be tilted towards <em>m2</em>. It's a weighted sum that gives a certain coordinate. There is nothing present at that location. There's nobody there. All the stuff is either here or there. The center of mass is the location of a mathematical entity. It's not a physical entity. If you go there and say, "What's at the center of mass?" you typically won't find anything. And it behaves like a body. After all, if you just said, "I've learned Newton's laws," and I walk into this room and I say this, you will say "Well, this guy's talking about a body of mass, capital <em>M</em>, undergoing some acceleration due to the force." So, the center of mass is the body whose mass seems to be the total mass of these two particles, whose acceleration is controlled by the same as Newton's law, but the right-hand side contains only the external forces; this is the key. All the internal forces have canceled out, and what remains is the external force.</p><p>Now it turns, if you've got three bodies, you can do a similar manipulation. And again, you'll have <em>F12</em> and <em>F23</em> and <em>F32</em> and so on. They will cancel and what will remain will be a similar thing, but this is the total external force. So, if I can say this in words, what we have learned is that the advantage of introducing a quantity called "center of mass" is that it responds only to the total force; it doesn't care about internal forces.</p><p>So, I'll give an example. Here is some airplane, right? It's in flight, and a couple of guys are having a fight, punching each other and so on. The rest of the passengers say "enough is enough" and they throw them out. So, they're just floating around, affecting each other's dynamics, and of course this person will feel a force due to that person, that person will feel a force due to this person, but what I'm telling you is the center of mass is going to drop like a rock. It's going to accelerate with the force <em>mgh</em>; it's going to accelerate with <em>g</em>. So, at one point this person may be having the upper hand and may be here, and the other person may be down here, but follow the center of mass and you'll find it simply falls under gravity. So, the mutual forces do not affect the dynamics of the center of mass. Or, for example, suppose at some point, this person blows the other one up into, say, it's a samurai bat, make it simple, cuts him up in two pieces, so now we've got three bodies now: the first protagonist and the other two now, unfortunately somewhat decimated. Now, you can take these three bodies, find their center of mass; it'll be the same thing; it'll just keep falling down. So, even though the system is becoming more and more complicated, you cannot change the dynamics of the center of mass. It responds only to the external force. If this fight was taking place in outer space where there's no gravity, then as this fight continues and people are flying and parts are flying everywhere, the center of mass will just be in one location, not doing anything. Yes?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> Couldn't the internal forces change the center of mass's location?</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> No, that's what I'm saying. The center of mass, if it changes it can certainly-- No one says the center of mass cannot accelerate. It can accelerate due to external forces. But if there were no external forces, then the center of mass will behave like a particle with no force. If it's not moving to begin with, it won't move later. Or if it is moving to begin with, it'll maintain a constant velocity.</p><p>So, here's another example. Now you can obviously generalize this to more than one dimension. If you're living in two dimensions, you will introduce an <em>x</em> coordinate and introduce a <em>y</em> coordinate and then you will have the center of mass as <em>MR</em> double dot equals <em>F</em>, and <em>R</em> would be <em>m1r1 + m2r2</em> divided by the total mass; <em>r1</em> and <em>r2</em> are just the location now in two dimensions of these two masses. So, here is <em>m1</em> and here is <em>m2</em> and the center of mass you can check will be somewhere in between the line joining the two points, but it'll now be a vector.</p><p>So here's another example. You take a complicated object; it's got masses and it's got springs; it's connected with thread, and chains and everything. You throw the whole mess into the air. All the different parts of it are jiggling and doing complicated movements, but if you follow the center of mass, in other words at every instant you take the <em>m1r1 + m2r2 + m3r3</em> and so on, divided by the total mass, that coordinate will simply be following the parabolic path of a body curving under gravity. If at some point this complicated object fragments into two chunks, one will land here and one will land there. But at every instant, if you follow the center of mass, it'll go as if nothing happened and it will land here. The center of mass does not care about internal forces, only about external forces. That's the main point. And it was designed in such a way that external [correction: should have said "internal"] forces canceled in these dynamics. So, everything I'm going to do today is to take that equation, <em>MX..= F</em> or <em>MR..= F</em>, in vector form, and deduce some of the consequences.</p><p>Now, first of all, you should realize that if you've got several bodies, say three bodies, then I will define the center of mass to be <em>mixi</em> divided by the sum of <em>mi</em>. This is a shorthand, I'm going to write it only once, but you should know what the notation means. If there is <em>i</em> from 1 to 3, it really means <em>m1x1 + m2x2 + m3x3</em> divided by <em>m1 + m2 + m3</em>. This summation is the notation mathematicians have introduced where the index <em>i</em> will go over a range from 1 to 3. Every term you let <em>i</em> take three different values and you do the sum. An exercise I've given to you guys to pursue at home is the following: if I got three bodies, 1, 2 and 3, you've defined the center of mass, you can either go to this formula, do all the <em>m1x1</em>'s and add them up, or you also have the following option. You can pick any two of them, say the first two -- forget the third one -- take these two, find their center of mass, let's call it <em>x1</em> and <em>x2</em> and with that total mass <em>M12</em>, which is just <em>m1 + m2</em>, trade these two for a new fictitious object and put that here, and forget these two. But on that one point it deposits the mass of these two; now, you take the center of mass of this object with the third object, by the same weighting process, <em>m3x3 + M12X12</em> divided by the total mass; you'll get the same answer as here.</p><p>What I'm telling you is, if you've got many bodies and you want the center of mass of all of them, you can take a subset of them, replace them by their center of mass, namely, all their mass sitting at their center of mass, replace the other half by their mass sitting at their center of mass, and finally find the center of mass of these two centers of mass, properly weighted, and that'll give you this result.</p><p>Okay, so, before I exploit that equation and find all the consequences, we have to get used to finding center of mass for a variety of things, as long as they give you ten masses, or a countable number of masses, we've just got to plug it in here; it's a very trivial exercise. Things become more interesting if I give you not a set of discrete masses but discrete locations, namely, a countable set of masses, but I give you a rod like this. This is a rod of mass <em>M</em> and length <em>L</em>, and I say: "Where is the center of mass?" So, we have to adapt the definition that we have for this problem.</p><p>So, what should I do? Well, this is my origin of coordinates. If I had a set of masses with definite locations I know how to do it, but this is a continuum. The trick then is to say, I take a distance <em>x</em> from the left hand, and I cut myself a very thin sliver of taking this <em>dx</em>. That sliver has got a certain mass, and I argue it's at a definite distance <em>x</em> from the coordinate's origin. And if you're nitpicking you will say, "What do you mean by definite distance?" It's got a width <em>dx</em>, so one part of it is at <em>x</em>, the other part is at <em>x + dx</em> so it doesn't have a definite coordinate. But if <em>dx</em> is going to 0, this argument will eventually be invalid. So <em>dx</em> goes to 0, sliver has a definite location, which is just the <em>x</em> coordinate of where I put it. So, to find the center of mass, which consists of multiplying every mass by its location and adding--Let me first find how much mass is sitting here. Let me call it <em> Δm</em>. How much mass is sitting there? Well, I do the following. I take the total mass and divide it by <em>L</em>; that's the mass per unit length. And this fellow has a width <em>dx</em>, so the mass of this little sliver is <em>(M/L) dx</em>.</p><p>Therefore, the center of mass that I want is found by taking this sliver of that mass, multiplying by its coordinate and summing over all the slivers, which is what we do by the integral from 0 to <em>L</em>. Then, I should divide by the total mass, which is just <em>M</em>. You can see now if you do this calculation. I get 1/<em>L</em>; then, I get integral <em>xdx</em> from 0 to <em>L</em>, and that's going to be <em>L2</em> over 2. So, if you do that you'll get <em>L</em>/2. I'm not doing every step in the calculus because at this point we should be able to do this without every detail. So, the center of mass of this rod, to nobody's surprise, is right in the midpoint, but it assumes that the rod is uniform, whereas [if its] like a baseball bat, thicker at one end and thinner at the other end, of course no one is saying that, but we have assumed the mass per unit length, namely <em>M</em> or is this a fixed number, <em>M/L</em>, and then this is the answer.</p><p>But there are other ways to get this result without doing all the work, okay? So, we would like to learn that other method because it'll save you a lot of time. It must be clear to most people that the center of mass of this rod is at the center. But how do we argue that? How do you make it official? If you do the integral you will get the answer, but I want to short circuit the integral. And here is a trick. It's not going to work for arbitrary bodies. If I give you some crazy object like this, you cannot do anything. But this is a very symmetric object; you can sort of tell if I take the midpoint. There is as much stuff to the right as to the left and somehow you want to make that argument formal, and you do the following.</p><p>Suppose I have a bunch of masses, and the object's really not even regular, and this is my origin of coordinates. If I replace every <em>x</em> by <em>-x</em>, okay--sorry, I should change this object, so this really looks like this. Here's the object. Suppose I replace every <em>x</em> by <em>-x</em> that's reflecting the body around this axis, it will look like this; it'll be jutting to the right instead of the left. So, don't go by my diagrams. You know what I'm trying to do. I'm trying to draw the mirror image of this object the other way. Then, I think it's clear to everybody, if I do that, <em>X</em> will go to <em>-X</em>, because in this averaging <em>mixi</em>, sum of all the masses, if every <em>x</em> goes to <em>-x</em> the center of mass will go to <em>-X</em>. But now, take this rod and transport every particle to its negative coordinate. And you take that guy and put it here, the rod looks the same. If the rod looks the same, the center of mass must look the same. That means <em>-xX</em> has to be equal to <em>x</em> itself and the only answer is <em>X</em> = 0. So, without doing any detailed calculation, you argue that the answer is <em>X</em> = 0.</p><p>To do this, of course, you must cleverly pick your coordinates so that the symmetry of the body is evident. If you took the body like this and you took a reflection around this point, it goes into body flipped over. There is not much you can say about it. So, what you really want to do is to pick a point of reflection so that upon reflection the body looks the same; the body looks the same, the answer must be the same. But if you argue the answer must be minus of itself, therefore the answer is 0. This is how the center of mass of symmetric bodies can be found. So, we know the answer for this rod.</p><p>Suppose I give you not a thin rod, but a rod of non-0 width. We want to know its center of mass; we're not going to do any more work now. By symmetry, I can argue that this has to be the center of mass, because I can take every point here and turn it into the point there by changing <em>y</em> to <em>-y</em>; therefore, capital <em>Y</em> will become minus capital <em>Y</em>, but the body looks the same after this mapping. So, capital <em>Y</em> is 0, and similarly capital <em>X</em> is 0, and that's the center of mass.</p><p>Okay, now, what if I give you this object, anybody want to try that? Would you guys like to try this? Yes, can you tell me where the center of mass should be, yeah? No, no, the guy in front of you, yes.</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> The center of mass, you can't get the center of mass with two objects, and then this is where you said over in the curve, find the center between those two masses.</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> Okay, is that what your answer was? Okay, so the correct answer is, replace this mass by all of its mass, whatever it is, sitting here. Replace this one by all of its mass sitting here; then, forget the big bodies, replace them by points. Then, he's got two masses located here, and you can find the weighted average. It may be somewhere there.</p><p>Okay, now let's take one more object. Then I'm pretty much done with finding these centers of mass. The object I'm going to pick is a triangle that looks like this; it's supposed to be symmetric, even though I've drawn it this way. That is <em>b</em> and that is <em>b</em>, and that distance is <em>h</em>; let the mass be <em>M</em>. Where is the center of mass of this object? Again, by symmetry, you can tell that the <em>y</em> coordinate of the center of mass must lie on this line, because if I take <em>y</em> to <em>-y</em>, it maps onto itself so it looks the same. But it's supposed to reverse capital <em>Y</em>; therefore, <em>Y</em> is <em>-Y</em> and therefore it's 0; so, it's evidently lying somewhere on this line. I cannot do further calculations of this type by saying where it is on the line, because it has no longer a symmetry in the <em>x</em> direction; it's symmetric on the <em>y</em> after flipping <em>y</em>, but I cannot take <em>x</em> to <em>-x</em>. In fact, if I take <em>x</em> to <em>-x</em> this one looks like this, it doesn't map into itself. But I can pick any point here; if I take <em>x</em> to <em>-x</em>, the object looks different. It looks like that object and relating one object to another object is what I'm trying to do. I want to relate it to the same object. That cannot be done for <em>x</em>. It can be done for <em>y</em>; for <em>x</em> you've got to do some honest work.</p><p>The honest work we will do then is to take this thing, take a strip here, with location <em>x</em> and width <em>dx</em>, and the height of that strip here is <em>y</em>; <em>y</em> of course varies with <em>x</em>. So, I'm going to argue that to find the center of mass of this triangle I can divide it into vertical strips which are parallel to each other, and find the center of mass by adding the weighted average of all these things. For that, I need to know what's the mass of the shaded region. So, let's call it <em> Δm</em>. The mass of the shaded region is the mass per unit area. I'll find the area later on in terms of <em>b</em> and <em>h</em>, but this is mass per unit area. Then, I need to know the area of the strip. I'm going to give the answer because I don't have time to probe it. But you should think about what the answer for the area of the shaded region is. It's got a height 2<em>y</em>, and it's got the width <em>dx</em>. It's not quite a rectangle because the edges are slightly tapered, but when <em> Δx</em> goes to 0, it's going to look like a rectangle. So, the area is 2<em>y Δx</em>. But I don't want to write everything in terms of <em>y</em>. I want to write it in terms of <em>x</em>; then, I do similar triangles. Similar triangles tell me that <em>y/b</em> is <em>x/h</em>, namely, that triangle compared to that triangle tells me <em>y/b</em> is <em>x/h</em>. Therefore, the <em>y</em> here can be replaced by <em>bx/h</em>. So, that is the mass of the sliver here, and its center is obviously here, so that is a mass there, there's a mass there; I've got to do the weighted average of all of them. So remember, I don't just integrate this over <em>x</em>; that would just give me the mass of the body. I should multiply it by a further <em>x</em> and then do the integral. So, what I really want to do to find the center of mass <em>x</em>, is to take that mass I got, <em>M/A</em>, there is a 2, there's an <em>h</em>, there is a <em>b</em>, there is an <em>x</em> from there, and another <em>x</em>, because you have to multiply this by the <em>x</em> coordinate of this thing, because that's the coordinate of the center of mass of this. There are two <em>x</em>s, that's what you've got to remember. So, that should be integrated from 0 to <em>h</em>, that'll give me <em>h3</em>/3. So, I get <em>(2Mb/Ah)</em> times <em>h3</em> over 3.</p><p>Now, you know there is one more thing we have to do. We must replace the area of the triangle by ½ base times altitude, which is <em>bh</em>. I also forgot to divide everything by the mass, because the center of mass is this weighted average divided by the total mass, so I've got to divide by 1/<em>M</em>. Well, I claim, if you do this and cancel everything you will get the answer of 2/3<em>h</em>. Okay, so not surprisingly the center of mass of this is not halfway to the other end, but two-thirds of the way because it's top heavy; this side of it is heavier.</p><p>This is the level of calculus you should be able to do in this course, be able to take some body, slice it up in some fashion, and find the location of the center of mass. You combine symmetry arguments with actual calculation. For this sliver, by symmetry, you know the center of mass is at the center, you don't waste your time, but then when you add these guys there is no further symmetry you can use; you have to do the actual work.</p><p>So, what have I done so far? What I've done is point out to you that when you work with extended bodies, or more than one body, we can now treat the entire body, replace the body by a single point for certain purposes. The single point is called a center of mass, where it imagines all the mass concentrated at the center of mass. So, you have created a brand new entity which is fictitious. It has a mass equal to total mass. It has a location equal to the center of mass, and it moves in response to the total force. And it's not aware of internal forces, and that's what we want to exploit. I already gave you a clue as to what the implications are, but let me now take a thorough analysis of this basic equation <em>MR..= F</em>. We're just going to analyze the consequence. So there are several cases you can consider.</p><p>Case one: <em>F</em> external not equal to 0. So, these are two bodies subject to mutual force and to an outside force, but the simplest example I've already given to you -- but I'll repeat it -- we're not going to do this in great detail. We all know, if I fire a point mass like this, it will do that. What I'm now telling you is, if I take a complex body made of 20,000 parts, all connected to each other pushing and pulling, if you fling that crazy thing in the air it'll do all kinds of gyrations and jiggling as it moves around. But if you found its center of mass, the center of mass will follow simply a parabola, because the external force on it is just <em>Mg</em>. So, it'll be <em>MR..= mg</em> and that's just motion with constant acceleration in the <em>y</em> direction, and it's just a projectile problem. And I repeat once more, for emphasis, that if this object broke into two objects, typically what'll happen is one will fly there and one will land here, but at every instant if you found their center of mass you will find it proceeds as if nothing happened. For example, if you have an explosive device that blows them apart, and the pieces are all flying, but that's just coming from one part of the piece pushing on another part of the piece, but those forces are of no interest to us. As far as the external force goes, it is still gravity so the center of mass will continue traveling. Beyond that, I'm not going to do too much with this thing. So let me now go to Case II.</p><h3>Chapter 3. Law of Conservation of Momentum — Examples and Applications [00:32:05]</h3><p>Case II. If you want, case 2a. <em>F</em> external is equal to 0. What does it mean if <em>F</em> external is 0? That means this is 0. That means <em>MR.. = 0</em>, that means <em>MR.</em> is a constant because it's not changing. Who is this <em>MR.</em>? What does it stand for? Well, it looks like the following. If you take a single particle of mass <em>m</em>, and velocity <em>x.</em>, we use the symbol <em>p</em>, maybe I've never used it before in the course, and that's called the momentum. The momentum of a body is this peculiar combination of mass and velocity. In fact, in terms of momentum we may write Newton's law. Instead of saying it's <em>mdv/dt</em>, which is <em>ma</em>, you can also write it as <em>d</em> by <em>dt</em> of <em>mv</em>, because <em>m</em> is a constant and you can take it inside the derivative, and that we can write as <em>dp/dt</em>. Sometimes, instead of saying force is mass times acceleration, people often say "force is the rate of change of momentum." The rate at which the momentum of a body is changing is the applied force. So, if I've not introduced to you the notion of momentum, well, here it is. So, if you think about it that way, this looks like the momentum of the center of mass, and we are told the momentum of the center of mass does not change if there are no external forces. But the momentum of the center of mass has a very simple interpretation in terms of the parts that make up the center of mass; let's see what it is.</p><p>Let's go back here. Remember, let me just take two bodies and you will get the idea; it's <em>m1 + m2</em>, which is total <em>M</em>, and let's take just one dimension when it's <em>m1x1.+ m2x2.</em> over <em>m1 + m2</em>; that is what <em>Mx.</em> is. So, <em>m1 + m2</em> cancels here, and you find this is just <em>p1 + p2</em>. Let's use the symbol capital <em>P</em> for momentum of the center of mass. So, the momentum of the center of mass is the sum of the momentum of the two parts, but what you're learning is -- so let me write it one more time -- if <em>F</em> eternal is equal to 0, then <em>p1 + p2</em> does not change with time. This is a very, very basic and fundamental property, and it's in fact another result that survives all the revolutions of relativity and quantum mechanics, where what I've said for two bodies is true for ten bodies; you just do the summation over more terms.</p><p>So, let me say in words what I'm saying. Take a collection of bodies. At a given instant everything is moving; it's got its own velocity and its momentum, add up all the momenta. If you had one dimension, just add the numbers. If in two dimensions, add the vectors; you get a total momentum. That total momentum does not change if there are no outside forces acting on it. So, a classic example is two people are standing on ice. Their total momentum is 0 to begin with, and the ice is incapable of any force along the plane. It's going to support you vertically against gravity, but if it's frictionless it cannot do anything in the plane. Then, the claim is that if you and I are standing and we push against each other and we fly apart, my momentum has to be exactly the opposite of your momentum, because initially yours plus mine was 0; that cannot change because there are no external forces. If two particles are pushing against each other, they can only do so without changing the total. Okay, so <em>p1 + p2</em> does not change, and here's another context in which it's important.</p><p>Suppose there is a mass <em>m1</em>, going with some velocity <em>v1</em>, and here's the second mass <em>m2</em>, going with some velocity <em>v2</em>; they collide. When they collide, all kinds of things can happen. I mean, <em>m1</em> may bump its head on that and come backwards, or it could be a heavy object that pushes everything in the forward direction, or at the end of the day you will have some <em>m1</em> going with a new velocity <em>v1'</em>, and <em>m2</em> going with a new velocity <em>v2'</em>. But what I'm telling you is that <em>m1 v1 + m2 v2</em> will be equal to <em>m1 v1' + m2 v2'</em>. In a collision, of course, one block exerts a force on the other block, and the other block exerts an opposite force on this block, and that's the reason why even though individually the momenta could be very different, finally the momenta will add up to the same total. Here's a simple example; you can show that if this mass and that mass are equal, and say this one is at rest, that one comes and hits this. You can show under certain conditions this one will come to rest and this will start moving with the speed of the--the target will move at the speed of the projectile. So, momenta of individual objects have changed. One was moving before, it is not moving; one was at rest, it's moving, but when you add up the total, it doesn't change.</p><p>This is called the Law of Conservation of Momentum. So, that's so important I'm just going to write it down here one more time. And the basic result is, if external forces are 0, then <em>p1 + p2 + p3</em> and so on, "before" will be <em>p1' + p2' + p3'</em>, and so on, where this means "before" and that means "after," . When is "before" and when is "after." Pick any two times in the life of these particles, it's like Law of Conservation of Energy, where we said <em>E1 = E2</em>, there 1 and 2 stood for "before" and "after." Well, here we cannot use 1 and 2 for "before" and "after" because 1 and 2 and 3 are labeling particles. So, the "before" quantities are written without a′, and the "after" quantities are written with a prime.</p><p>Everybody follow this? It's very important you follow this statement and follow the conditions under which it's valid. There cannot be external forces. For example, in the collision of these two masses, if there is friction between the blocks and the table, you can imagine they collide and they both come to rest after a while. Originally, they had momentum and finally they don't. What happened? Well, here you have an explanation, namely, the force of friction was an external force acting on them. What I'm saying is that if the only force on each block is the one due to each other, then the total momentum will not change. So, the case that I considered, 2a, was external force equal to 0, but center of mass was moving, because it had a momentum. Then, the claim is that momentum will not change.</p><p>I'm coming to the last case, which is, if you want, case 2b. The external forces are 0, the center of mass was 0; in other words, center of mass was at rest. If you find these different cases complicated, then I don't mind telling you one more time. The center of mass behaves like a single object responding to the external force. It's clear that if the external force is non-zero, the center of mass will accelerate. If the external force is 0, the center of mass will not accelerate. There are cases 1 and 2. 2a and 2b are the following: if it does not accelerate, its velocity will not change. So then, you have the two cases, it had a velocity, which it maintained, or it had no velocity, in which case it does not even move. See, if you apply <em>F = ma</em> to a body and there are no forces, you cannot say the body will be at rest. You will say the body will maintain the velocity. So, if it had a velocity, it'll go at the velocity, if it was at rest it'll remain at rest; the same goes for the center of mass. If the center of mass was moving, it'll preserve its momentum. That really means the sum of the momenta of the individual pieces will be preserved. If it was at rest, since the external force is 0, it will remain at rest. So, I want to look at the consequence of this one. I could've done them in either order. I can take the case where there's no external force, there is no motion, or I chose to do with the opposite way, where I took the most complicated case, where external force is not 0. Then, I took the case where it is 0 but the center of mass was moving to begin with, and therefore it has to keep moving no matter what. And the simplest case is the center of mass was at rest; then, it's not moving now and it will never move.</p><p>So, let me give an example of where the idea comes into play. We looked at the planetary motion of the Sun and the Earth, and I said the Earth goes around the Sun, so let's look at it a little later; there's the Earth and the only force between the Earth and the Sun is the mutual force of gravitation. Now, my question to you is, "Is this picture of the Sun sitting here and the Earth moving around acceptable or not in view of what I've said?" Yes?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> The Sun and Earth revolve around a mutual center of gravity.</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> Yes, that's the answer to the problem. But what is wrong if I just say the Sun remains here and the Earth goes in a circle, which is what we accepted last time?</p><p><strong>Student:</strong> The momentum of the Sun doesn't change, but it changes in the momentum of the Earth.</p><p><strong>Professor Ramamurti Shankar:</strong> That's one way. Do you understand what he said? He said the momentum of the Sun is not changing. The momentum of the Earth is changing, so the

	<div class="node__content session-full__content">
		<h2 class="session-full__title">
			Lecture 9
			-
			Rotations, Part I: Dynamics of Rigid Bodies
		</h2>
		<div class="session-full__body">
			<h3 class="session-full__body-label">
				Overview
			</h3>
			<p>Part I of Rotations. The lecture begins with examining rotation of rigid bodies in two dimensions. The concepts of "rotation" and "translation" are explained. The use of radians is introduced. Angular velocity, angular momentum, angular acceleration, torque and inertia are also discussed. Finally, the Parallel Axis Theorem is expounded.</p>
